web_evidence.note: Publisher metadata verifies the title, author, 2005 publication, and prose-fiction eligibility, but its synopsis does not establish narrative person.

web_evidence.title: The Camel Club by David Baldacci | Excerpt | Bookreporter.com
web_evidence.note: A sustained Chapter 1 excerpt, explicitly reprinted with publisher permission, narrates Oliver Stone externally as he/he/Stone and enters his memories and thoughts. Local first-person thoughts and dialogue remain embedded within that third-person frame.

web_evidence.title: The Camel Club Chapters 24-35 | SuperSummary
web_evidence.note: The structural analysis describes shifting perspectives across Stone, Alex, Hemingway, Djamila, and Captain Jack while calling the reader's observing position omniscient. It also identifies the humans-are-rotten passage as Captain Jack's speech, resolving the apparent first-person conflict in q01149.

web_evidence.title: The Camel Club Chapters 60-70 | SuperSummary
web_evidence.note: The closing-chapter analysis continues to describe an external narrative that moves among Gray, Hemingway, Stone, Alex, and other characters and gives access to their distinct motivations.

search_log: Searched "The Camel Club" "David Baldacci" with official excerpt, first chapter, publisher, author, and reading-guide terms; found the permissioned Bookreporter Chapter 1 excerpt and Hachette title record.
Searched title plus point of view, third person, narrator, and omniscient; found SuperSummary's explicit analysis of shifting perspectives and an omniscient observing position.

Opened Google Books, Open Library, and OverDrive records. Their previews or samples were unavailable to the text browser or exposed only metadata/isolated sentences, so they were not used as person evidence.

Searched the exact q01149 language, including "I've fought for and against pretty much every cause there is" and "humans are rotten to the core"; Goodreads reproduced the quotation, while SuperSummary's Chapter 25 account established that the sentiment belongs to Captain Jack's dialogue.
Searched title plus epistolary, diary, frame narrative, multiple narrators, alternating narration, and first person; found no credible evidence of sustained first- or second-person base sections.
person_note: The permissioned opening and the interior Goodreads passages independently show a nonparticipating third-person narrator with access to several characters' thoughts. The book shifts focal characters and plotlines, but the grammatical narrating person remains third, so this is not ALTERNATING. q01149's apparent first person is Captain Jack's speech, and other first-person forms occur in dialogue or free-direct thought. Several clipped quotes remain locally nondiagnostic, but no credible source indicates a competing base person; the main limitation is that the authorized prose source covers only the opening, mitigated by multiple interior passages and structural coverage through the final chapters.
